structure.title: Act I · Athens · Fathers, dukes and amateur actors
structure.text: Hermia's father wants the duke to enforce his choice of husband. Elsewhere craftsmen cast a wedding entertainment. One group flees the city's authority and the other seeks its applause. They choose the same wood.

structure.title: Act II – Act IV, scene 1 · The wood · A badly managed intervention
structure.text: The fairy rulers' quarrel spills over into human courtship. A flower applied to a sleeper's eyes rearranges desire more quickly than anyone can explain a change of heart. The rehearsing actors have their own reasons to worry about appearances.

structure.title: Act IV, scene 2 – Act V · Athens again · The wedding audience
structure.text: The court has heard an extraordinary story about the night. It now watches a group of tradesmen attempt to stage the deaths of two lovers. The sophisticated audience gets its own chance to be ridiculous.

people.name: Lysander and Demetrius
people.role: Two young Athenians in love with Hermia
people.text: Hermia's father has chosen Demetrius; Hermia has chosen Lysander, and Demetrius once courted Helena. When the lovers run into the woods at night, the fairies' interference makes the two men even harder to tell apart.

people.name: Hermia and Helena
people.text: Childhood intimacy has given them a whole private history. When the men's affections start jumping about, each woman can imagine a particularly painful explanation involving the other.

people.name: Bottom and his company
people.text: Bottom volunteers for more parts than any production could give him. His colleagues take seriously the possibility that a lion onstage might upset somebody. Their anxiety about the audience displays a touching degree of consideration.

context.title: Two courts with domestic troubles
context.text: The duke's upcoming marriage frames the action. In the wood, Oberon and Titania are already married and fiercely at odds over a child. The fairies possess extraordinary powers and a very familiar ability to make their quarrel everyone else's business.

notice.text: Listen to lovers describing what their eyes tell them.
notice.why: The poetry can sound equally sincere before and after the magic takes effect. Helena has excellent reasons for suspecting that an unexpected declaration is a practical joke.
The tradesmen repeatedly interrupt their fiction to explain it. Their audience keeps interrupting too, and its jokes sometimes display a more painful failure of imagination.

opening: Hermia must marry the man her father chooses or face a punishment she cannot accept. She runs into the woods with the man she loves, followed by two people whose desires make the situation worse. The fairies living there have a marriage dispute of their own and access to something human lovers lack: a way to change whom someone wants. By morning, love will have produced magnificent declarations, atrocious behaviour, and very little evidence that anyone understands what has happened to them.
